planting.note: Set out after last frost in a sheltered, high-light spot with rich, well-drained soil; this cool-tropical species tolerates brief light frost once established but needs a long frost-free stretch to flower and fruit.

directions: This high-elevation Andean vine produces elongated, bright yellow fruit filled with aromatic orange pulp, prized in Colombia and Ecuador for juice and desserts under the name curuba. It was only recently split taxonomically from the closely related Passiflora tripartita var. mollissima and Passiflora mollissima, and it struggles in prolonged summer heat, preferring a cool-summer or high-elevation subtropical climate. Give it a sturdy arbor or fence, humus-rich soil, and consistent moisture, and expect the first fruit roughly one to one-and-a-half years after planting a rooted cutting or seedling. Because it can naturalize aggressively in mild, moist climates, check local invasive-species lists before planting.

planting.note: Plant the entire fruit on its side with the stem end barely covered, exactly as with smooth chayote; this spiny selection needs the same warm, frost-free start.

directions: Unlike the smooth, spineless chayote types more common in US markets, this traditional Mesoamerican and Caribbean varietal group bears fruit covered in soft to firm spines and is often preferred in Mexican, Central American, and Caribbean cooking for its firmer texture. Grow it exactly as common chayote, planting the whole fruit at a slight angle in rich soil and training the vigorous vine onto a heavy-duty trellis or arbor, since a single plant can cover 400 square feet or more. Wear gloves when handling and harvesting the fruit, as the spines can be sharp on some selections, though many are only softly bristled. In frost-free zones the vine is a long-lived perennial that also produces an edible starchy tuberous root after a few seasons.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 2-3 weeks early; provide sturdy trellising immediately as vines grow quickly and can reach 10-12 feet.

directions: Bolivian Giant is a large-fruited achocha selection popularized by UK seed savers, bearing smooth to lightly spined, hollow fruit noticeably bigger than the standard species type and well suited to stuffing whole. The vigorous, tendril-climbing vine easily covers 10 to 12 feet of trellis or fence in a single season and produces heavily even in cooler summers where cucumbers struggle. Harvest fruit while still young and tender, before the interior seeds harden and blacken, for the best crisp, mild, cucumber-like flavor. Because the plant self-seeds readily and can naturalize in mild climates, remove spent vines at season's end if volunteer seedlings are unwanted.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors on their sides 4-6 weeks before last frost at a warm 73-80F for reliable germination; transplant out after all frost danger has passed and nights stay warm.

directions: Fat Baby is a compact, early-fruiting achocha selection with softer spines and smaller, rounder fruit than the typical Cyclanthera brachystachya type, reaching harvestable size in as little as two months from transplanting. Its quicker maturity and gentler spines make it one of the easier achocha types for short-season or cool-summer gardens. Train the twining vine onto netting or a trellis, where it climbs vigorously by tendrils and sets fruit continuously if picked young and often. Slice or stuff the immature, hollow fruit as a mild, crunchy cucumber substitute; older fruit toughens and its black seeds become bitter.

common_name: Silver Moon Hyacinth Bean (White Hyacinth Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost into warm soil, or start indoors 3-4 weeks early for an earlier bloom; provide a tall trellis or fence for the fast twining vine.

directions: Silver Moon is the white-flowered counterpart to the familiar purple Ruby Moon hyacinth bean, producing upright wands of pure white blossoms followed by pale, silvery-green seed pods that shimmer against the green foliage. Like other hyacinth beans it is a fast, twining vine that thrives in summer heat and humidity, flowering from midsummer until frost and drawing in pollinators. Give it a sturdy trellis, arbor, or fence to climb, consistent moisture, and full sun for the heaviest bloom and pod set. As with other ornamental lablab types, treat the raw pods and seeds as toxic and grow it strictly as an ornamental screen or cut-flower vine rather than a food crop.

common_name: Highworth Lablab (Early Hyacinth Bean Forage Cultivar)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; Highworth flowers and sets seed earlier than late-season types like Rongai, making it a better fit for regions with shorter frost-free windows.

directions: Highworth is an early-flowering Lablab purpureus cultivar bred in Australia from South Indian germplasm specifically to set seed before autumn frosts arrive, unlike later-maturing types such as Rongai. It bears purple flowers and black seed and is grown as a vigorous, twining warm-season cover crop and forage legume that fixes nitrogen, suppresses weeds, and can be grazed, cut for hay, or turned in as green manure. Direct sow into warm soil after the last frost and provide some support or allow it to sprawl as a dense ground-covering tangle. Because it matures earlier than most lablab types, Highworth suits gardeners and farmers in cooler regions or shorter growing seasons who want a reliable seed set.

planting.note: Direct-sow seed 1 inch deep after soil has thoroughly warmed and all frost danger has passed, providing a sturdy trellis for the vigorous climbing vines.

directions: This Taiwanese-type bitter melon produces oblong fruit that opens pale green and ripens to a smooth, ivory-white skin, a milder-tasting and visually striking alternative to the typical dark green Chinese and Indian types. Fruits run 6-9 inches long and about 3 inches across, with noticeably less bitterness than most bitter melon selections, making it a good introduction to the crop for first-time growers. Grow it on a sturdy trellis in full sun with consistent moisture, and harvest while the skin is still firm and pale rather than letting it soften and yellow. It has become popular in West Coast Asian markets, commanding a premium price over standard green types.
